thread.title: CSG passes Divestment for Humanity Act again
thread.title_full: CSG passes Divestment for Humanity Act again

author: Angel Saade
title: CSG passes Divestment for Humanity Act again
text:
The University of Michigan Central Student Government met Tuesday evening in the Wolverine Room of the Michigan Union to discuss community participation in CSG meetings and the Divest for Humanity Act.
The meeting began with a presentation to the Student Assembly from Spectrum Center director Jesse Beal and Spencer Hall, support services and wellness advocate, about the importance of having an inclusive space for LGBTQ+ students and highlighting the mental health crisis among young Queer individuals. Beal said for LGBTQ+ students, having even one supportive adult is enough to reduce the chance of suicide.
“If you have one affirming adult in your life and you’re a Queer (or) (transgender) youth, your chance of suicide decreases by 40%,” Beal said. “Affirming peers, mentors, communities … research and scholarship tells us these are protective factors that decrease suicidality, depression, anxiety (and) self-harm.”
The Assembly then voted to indefinitely table a motion to recall Law School student Keethan Kleiner, CSG representative, who was not present at the meeting. A motion to recall is automatically called after four unexcused absences.
During the community concerns portion, 21 students, staff, alumni and community members spoke in favor of passing AR 15-051, Divest for Humanity Act. The resolution comes in response to the Israel’s military campaign military campaign in Gaza, which has killed more than 69,000 people and has been classified as a genocide by the United Nations and various human rights organizations.
The resolution urges the University’s Board of Regents to form a committee to investigate the University’s financial ties to the Israeli government and initiate divestment procedures similar to the ones used by the University to divest from Apartheid South Africa in 1978.
The act was initially passed this fall but was vetoed by LSA and Education senior Eric Veal Jr., CSG President, in November. CSG’s Human Rights Party bypassed Veal Jr.’s veto by creating a petition garnering more than 1,700 signatures, allowing the act to be reconsidered by the Student Assembly.
University alum Gregg Krupa said if the Assembly upholds their land acknowledgement, they will support the passing of the Divest for Humanity Act.
“You pledge at each meeting to help make things right for Indigenous people … (and) hold the University of Michigan accountable,” Krupa said. “No one is more indigenous than the Palestinians in Palestine. If you believe in what you say about holding the University accountable for the treatment of Indigenous people, you will vote (yes) tonight. If you do not, you are obligated to explain why you pledge one thing, and when it comes to Palestinians, do another.”
The Assembly then entered debate on the resolution. LSA senior Keshava Demerath-Shanti, CSG representative and one of the resolution’s sponsors, said the resolution cites facts regarding the University’s policies and international human rights findings.
“It is unbecoming of the student government of one of the best, if not the best, public universities in the world, to deny the findings of the experts on human rights,” Demerath-Shanti said. “This matters because we have a responsibility to humanity. It also matters because it matters to students on this campus. (We collected) those hundreds of signatures for this petition when it was vetoed by the person who’s supposed to represent our campus.”
Business senior Jason Nuridjanian, CSG representative, said his main reason for disagreement with the bill is its supposed political intent and timing.
“The way (the resolution) has been framed is near an election where if it passes, you can claim it as an achievement,” Nuridjanian said. “Only for you to shut down the government which actually cuts off resources to other clubs. If it fails, you can play the card of basically saying ‘Look what they’ve done. They don’t care about the issue.’”
Dentistry student Christina Jones, CSG representative and one of the resolution’s sponsors, said the bill was not placed for political purposes and that it is simply how the timing worked out.
“We didn’t hold out on signatures so that we could politically time this,” Jones said. “We’ve talked, we’ve had dialogue. It’s time to take action. At the end of the day, if all we have is conversation, we’re just stalling the issue. Justice delayed is justice denied.”
The resolution passed in a secret ballot with 19 in favor and seven against. Because the vote was a reconsideration, the Divest for Humanity Act cannot be vetoed.
AR 15-096, Resolution Workshop Adjustment; AR 15-091, Heating The Bus Stops; and AR 15-098, Impeachment Notification Act, which requires the Speaker to be notified of any impeachment articles at least 48 hours prior to the Assembly meeting, were all passed unanimously.
AR 15-099, Community Concerns Eligibility Act, was introduced. The act would require that any person who wishes to speak during Assembly meetings is a student, faculty or staff member at the University, limiting the ability of Ann Arbor residents or alumni to partake in community concerns.
Engineering junior Alex Partlan, CSG representative, said he believes only University-affiliated individuals should be granted speaking power at Assembly meetings.
“We are elected to represent the student body,” Partlan said. “Our all-campus constitution protects the rights of students and nobody else — we don’t represent faculty, students (or) alumni. We don’t represent people who don’t have any affiliation with the University. This is important to make sure we are only hearing from people who are actually affected by what we do here.”
Rackham student Erin Neely, CSG representative, said she believes the bill is unnecessary and limits speech.
“We have not had much disruption from members of the community to justify closing the forum of community concerns,” Neely said. “Actually, we have the opposite problem. We rarely have people show up. … I would not test how far we can go in regulating speech. At the very least, this is violating the spirit of the all campus all-campus constitution.”
AR 15-099 was referred to the Rules Committee for a second read.
The Assembly passed CA 15-007, Safeguarding Student Organizations Amendment, unanimously. This would require CSG to spend a minimum of 30% of student fee revenue from fall and winter semesters on funding for student organizations. The constitutional amendment will be considered by the student body during the winter 2026 CSG elections on March 25 and March 26.
Daily News Staffer Angel Saade can be reached at angelsaa@umich.edu.
